title: Christians help the emperor by prayer
source_text: Εἶθ᾿ ἑξῆς προτρέπεται ἡμᾶς ὁ Κέλσος ἀρήγειν τῷ βασιλεῖ παντὶ σθένει καὶ συμπονεῖν αὐτῷ τὰ δίκαια καὶ ὑπερμαχεῖν αὐτοῦ καὶ συστρατεύειν αὐτῷ, ἂν ἐπείγῃ, καὶ συστρατηγεῖν. λεκτέον δὲ καὶ πρὸς ταῦτα ὅτι ἀρήγομεν κατὰ καιρὸν τοῖς βασιλεῦσι θείαν, ἵν᾿ οὕτως εἴπω, ἄρηξιν, καὶ „πανοπλίαν“ ἀναλαμβάνοντες „θεοῦ.“ καὶ ταῦτα ποιοῦμεν πειθόμενοι ἀποστολικῇ φωνῇ λεγούσῃ· „παρακαλῶ οὖν ὑμᾶς πρῶτον ποιεῖσθαι δεήσεις, προσευχὰς, ἐντεύξεις, εὐχαριστίας ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀνθρώπων, ὑπὲρ βασιλέων καὶ πάντων τῶν ἐν ὑπεροχῇ ὄντων.“ καὶ ὅσῳ γε τὶς εὐσεβέστερός ἐστι, τοσούτῳ ἀνυτικώτερος ἐν τῷ ἀρήγειν τοῖς βασιλεύουσι παρὰ τοὺς εἰς τὰς παρατάξεις ἐξιόντας στρατιώτας καὶ ἀναιροῦντας οὓς ἂν δύνωνται τῶν πολεμίων. εἶτα δὲ καὶ ταῦτ᾿ εἴποιμεν ἂν πρὸς τοὺς ἀλλοτρίους τῆς πίστεως καὶ ἀξιοῦντας ἡμᾶς στρατεύεσθαι ὑπὲρ τοῦ κοινοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπους ἀναιρεῖν ὅτι καὶ οἱ καθ᾿ ὑμᾶς ἱερεῖς ἀγαλμάτων τινῶν καὶ νεωκόροι ὧν νομίζετε θεῶν τηροῦσιν ἑαυτῶν ἀμίαντον τὴν δεξιὰν διὰ τὰς θυσίας, ἵν᾿ ἀναιμάκτοις χερσὶ καὶ καθαραῖς ἀπὸ φόνων προσάγωσι τὰς νενομισμένας θυσίας οἷς φατε θεοῖς· καὶ οὐ δή που πολέμου καταλαβόντος καὶ τοὺς ἱερεῖς στρατεύετε. εἰ ουν τοῦτ᾿ εὐλόγως γίνεται. πόσῳ μᾶλλον ἄλλων στρατευομένων καὶ οὗτοι στρατεύονται ὡς ἱερεῖς τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ θεραπευταὶ, καθαρὰς μὲν τηροῦντες τὰς δεξιὰς ἀγωνιζόμενοι δὲ διὰ τῶν πρὸς θεὸν εὐχῶν ὑπὲρ τῶν δικαίως στρατευομένων καὶ ὑπὲρ τοῦ δικαίως βασιλεύοντος, ἵνα τὰ ἐναντία πάντα καὶ ἐχθρὰ τοῖς δικαίως πράττουσι καθαιρεθῇ; ἡμεῖς δὲ καὶ ταῖς εὐχαῖς πάντας δαίμονας. τοὺς ἐγείροντας τὰ πολεμικὰ καὶ ὅρκους συγχέοντας καὶ τὴν εἰρήνην ταράσσοντας, καθαιροῦντες μᾶλλον βοηθοῦμεν τοῖς βασιλεύουσιν ἤπερ οἱ δοκοῦντες στρατεύεσθαι. συμπονοῦμεν δὲ τοῖς κοινοῖς πράγμασιν οἱ μετὰ δικαιοσύνης ἀναφέροντες προσευχὰς, σὺν ἀσκήσεσι καὶ μελέταις διδασκούσαις καταφρονεῖν ἡδονῶν καὶ μὴ ἄγεσθαι ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν. ἡμεῖς καὶ μᾶλλον ὑπερμαχοῦμεν τοῦ βασιλέως· καὶ οὐ συστρατευόμεθα μὲν αὐτῷ, κἂν ἐπείγῃ, στρατευόμεθα δὲ ὑπὲρ αὐτοῦ ἴδιον στρατόπεδον εὐσεβείας συγκροτοῦντες διὰ τῶν πρὸς τὸ θεῖον ἐντεύξεων.
pass_a_gloss: Then next Celsus urges (προτρέπω) us to help (ἀρήγω) the king/emperor (βασιλεύς) with all strength (σθένος), and to labour with (συμπονέω) him in just things (τὰ δίκαια), and to fight for (ὑπερμαχέω) him, and to campaign with (συστρατεύω) him, if he presses (ἐπείγω), and to be a fellow-general (συστρατηγέω). It must be said also against these that we help in due time (κατὰ καιρόν) the kings with divine, so to speak, help (ἄρηξις), also taking up (ἀναλαμβάνω) the 'full armour (πανοπλία) of God'. And we do these things obeying (πείθομαι) the apostolic voice saying: 'I exhort you then first to make petitions (δέησις), prayers (προσευχή), intercessions (ἔντευξις), thanksgivings (εὐχαριστία) for all men, for kings and all those in eminence (ὑπεροχή)'. And by how much one is more pious (εὐσεβής), by so much more effective (ἀνυτικός) in helping those reigning than the soldiers going out to the battle-lines (παράταξις) and killing (ἀναιρέω) whom they can of the enemies. Then we would say these things also to those alien (ἀλλότριος) to the faith (πίστις) and demanding (ἀξιόω) that we soldier (στρατεύομαι) for the common (τὸ κοινόν) and kill men: that also the priests (ἱερεύς) among you of certain images (ἄγαλμα) and temple-wardens (νεωκόρος) of those you think gods keep their right hand undefiled (ἀμίαντος) because of the sacrifices (θυσία), so that with bloodless (ἀναίμακτος) hands, pure from murders (φόνος), they may offer the customary sacrifices to those you call gods; and surely, war having come upon (καταλαμβάνω), you do not enlist the priests too. If then this happens reasonably (εὐλόγως), how much more, others soldiering, do these also soldier as priests and attendants (θεραπευτής) of God, keeping their right hands pure, but contending (ἀγωνίζομαι) through prayers (εὐχή) to God for those justly soldiering and for the one justly reigning, so that all things contrary and hostile to those acting justly may be destroyed (καθαιρέω)? And we, by prayers destroying all demons (δαίμων) who rouse (ἐγείρω) warlike things and confound (συγχέω) oaths (ὅρκος) and disturb (ταράσσω) peace, help the reigning more than those who seem to soldier. And we labour with the common affairs, we who offer up (ἀναφέρω) prayers with righteousness (δικαιοσύνη), with ascetic exercises (ἄσκησις) and studies/meditations (μελέτη) teaching to despise (καταφρονέω) pleasures (ἡδονή) and not be led by them. We even more fight for the king; and we do not campaign with him, even if he presses, but we soldier on his behalf, assembling (συγκροτέω) our own army (στρατόπεδον) of piety (εὐσέβεια) through intercessions (ἔντευξις) to the divine (τὸ θεῖον).
pass_b_english: Next Celsus urges us to help the emperor with all our strength, to labour with him in what is just, to fight for him, to serve in his army if he presses us, and to share command with him.

To this too we must say that we do help emperors when there is need, with a help that is, so to speak, divine, and taking up “the whole armour of God” (Ephesians 6:13). And we do this in obedience to the apostle’s voice, which says: “I urge you, then, first to make petitions, prayers, intercessions and thanksgivings for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions” (1 Timothy 2:1–2). And the more pious a person is, the more effective he is in helping those who reign: more effective than the soldiers who go out to the battle lines and kill as many of the enemy as they can.

Then we might also say this to those who are strangers to the faith and who demand that we serve as soldiers for the common good and kill men: even among you, the priests of certain images and the temple-keepers of those you consider gods keep their right hands undefiled for the sake of the sacrifices, so that they may offer the customary sacrifices to those you call gods with hands free of blood and clean of killing; and surely, when war comes, you do not enlist the priests too. If, then, this is reasonably done, how much more reasonably, while others go to war, do these also wage their war as priests and servants of God, keeping their right hands clean but striving through prayers to God for those who fight in a just cause and for him who reigns justly, so that everything opposed and hostile to those who act justly may be overthrown?

And we, by our prayers overthrowing all the demons who stir up wars, break oaths and disturb peace, help those who reign more than those who seem to be soldiers do. We share the labours of public affairs, we who offer up prayers with righteousness, together with disciplines and meditations that teach us to despise pleasures and not to be led by them. We fight for the emperor even more; and we do not serve in his army, even if he presses us, but we wage war on his behalf, raising an army of our own, an army of piety, through our intercessions to the Deity.

choices.choice: The opening infinitives (help with all strength, labour with him in what is just, fight for him, serve with him if he presses, share command) report Celsus indirectly, as the Greek frames them; they are not put in quotation marks, though they probably keep his wording, since Origen echoes each verb in his reply (ἀρήγειν, συμπονεῖν, ὑπερμαχεῖν, συστρατεύειν, ἂν ἐπείγῃ). βασιλεύς in the singular is rendered ‘emperor’ (the Roman emperor is meant); the plural βασιλεῦσι ‘emperors’; οἱ βασιλεύοντες ‘those who reign’; in the Pauline quotation βασιλέων stays ‘kings’. ‘The whole armour of God’ (πανοπλίαν ἀναλαμβάνοντες θεοῦ) matches Ephesians 6:13 (ἀναλάβετε τὴν πανοπλίαν τοῦ θεοῦ); Ephesians 6:11 has the same noun. 1 Timothy 2:1–2: Origen’s form παρακαλῶ οὖν ὑμᾶς πρῶτον differs slightly from the NT’s παρακαλῶ οὖν πρῶτον πάντων. ὅρκους συγχέοντας rendered ‘break oaths’ (the standard sense of the phrase, as in Homer’s ὅρκια σύν ... ἔχευαν). τὸ θεῖον rendered ‘the Deity’. The staged text’s full stop after γίνεται is treated as a comma; the sentence beginning πόσῳ μᾶλλον is kept as a question, as printed, with εὐλόγως understood from the protasis (‘how much more reasonably’). ἂν ἐπείγῃ / κἂν ἐπείγῃ: subject taken as the emperor (‘if he presses us’); an impersonal ‘if need presses’ is also possible.
καὶ πανοπλίαν ἀναλαμβάνοντες: restored the καί ('and taking up')
1 Timothy 2:1: 'first of all' to 'first', matching Origen's πρῶτον without πάντων
ὅσῳ ... τοσούτῳ ἀνυτικώτερος ... παρά: removed the doubled 'more ... more so than'
πόσῳ μᾶλλον: made the a fortiori explicit ('how much more reasonably'), 'wage their war'
συμπονοῦμεν τοῖς κοινοῖς πράγμασιν: 'labour with the commonwealth' to 'share the labours of public affairs'
Ephesians 6:13 and 1 Timothy 2:1-2 checked against the Greek

choices.choice: 8.73: the subject of ἂν ἐπείγῃ / κἂν ἐπείγῃ is the emperor in this draft ('if he presses us'). An impersonal reading ('if need presses') is also possible. It is noted in the translator_notes, not changed.
